reconcile.connective: Defenders read Matthew's "fourteen generations" as a stylized mnemonic grouping rather than a literal head-count, pointing to comparable compressions elsewhere in Old Testament genealogies.

discrepancy.connective: The sharpest objection comes from Isaac of Troki, who charged that Matthew dropped Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah on purpose so the tally would come out to three even fourteens.

skeptic.name: Isaac of Troki
skeptic.attribution: Isaac of Troki (1533-1594), Chizzuk Emunah [Faith Strengthened], trans. Moses Mocatta (1851)

excerpts.excerpt_text: Such artificial aids to memory were familiar to the Jews, and much larger gaps than those here are found in some of the Old Testament genealogies. In Ezr 7:1-5 no fewer than six generations of the priesthood are omitted, as will appear by comparing it with Ch1 6:3-15.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: JFB's headline comment on Matt 1:17 explains the 'fourteen' figure as a stylized memory device with an OT genealogical precedent (Ezra) for large-scale omission of generations -- directly answers why Chronicles' fuller king-list can outrun Matthew's stated count.

pd_work.resource: John W. Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John W. Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats Matthew's three-fourteens directly under 'Generations, forty-two / A different number' (Matt. i.17 vs. i.2-16), citing the common Jewish practice of dividing genealogies by a 'favorite or mystical number' with generations repeated or left out, and naming theories for which kings Matthew omitted.
